listeningParts.title: Booking an ancient writing workshop
listeningParts.contextDescription: A woman phones a city museum to book a weekend workshop on ancient writing for herself and her daughter.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Good morning, Hallam City Museum, bookings desk. Owen speaking. How can I help?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Oh, hello. I picked up a leaflet about your weekend workshops on ancient writing, and I'd like to book a place for myself and my daughter, if there's still room.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Lovely. Where did you find the leaflet, just out of interest? We're trying to work out which kind of advertising actually works.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: It was at the library on the high street, on the noticeboard by the entrance.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: That's useful to know, thank you. Right, we have two different workshops running this month. One is called Clay and Reed, where you learn to write cuneiform on clay tablets, the way scribes did in ancient Mesopotamia. The other is called Ink and Papyrus, and that one's about Egyptian hieroglyphs. You paint them with a brush on a sheet of real papyrus.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: They both sound fascinating. Which one would suit a twelve-year-old better?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Both are suitable from age ten, so she'd be fine with either. But I'd say Clay and Reed is the more hands-on of the two. Everyone makes their own tablet from scratch, writes their name on it in cuneiform, and then takes it home to dry. The children usually love that part. The papyrus one is quieter and needs a very steady hand.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: She'd much prefer getting her hands dirty, I think. When is Clay and Reed?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: It runs on Saturday mornings. This month there are two sessions, on the eighth and the twenty-second. I'm afraid the eighth is already fully booked, but there are still a few places left on the twenty-second.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: The twenty-second is fine. We're free that weekend.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Great. The session starts at half past ten and finishes at one, so it's two and a half hours altogether, with a short break in the middle. It's worth arriving about ten minutes early, because the tutor starts promptly.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: And how much does it cost?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: For adults it's eighteen pounds, and for children under sixteen it's twelve. If you're members of the museum's Friends scheme, you get twenty per cent off, but otherwise it's the standard price.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: No, we're not members. So that's thirty pounds for the two of us, is it?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: That's right, thirty pounds in total.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Fine. Do we need to bring anything with us?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: All the materials are provided: the clay, the reed styluses, and a box to carry your tablet home in. But the clay is quite messy, and it can stain, so I'd strongly recommend wearing old clothes, or bringing an apron if you have one.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Good tip. What about food? Is there anywhere to eat?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: There's a café on the ground floor, and everyone taking part in a workshop gets a free drink there. You just show your ticket at the counter. It's included in the price, so you might as well use it.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Lovely. And where in the building is the workshop held?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: It's in the Learning Centre, which is on the second floor, right next to our gallery of Near Eastern antiquities. In fact, the session begins with a short tour of that gallery, and the tutor shows you some genuine tablets that are around four thousand years old, so you can see what you're trying to copy.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: That's a nice idea. Is there a lift? My daughter's fine, but I've got a bad knee at the moment.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Yes, there are two lifts just inside the main entrance. Now, could I take your name, please?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Yes, it's Fiona Delacourt. D-E-L-A-C-O-U-R-T.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Thank you. And your daughter's first name?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: It's Mia.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Lovely. I'll email the tickets to you once you've paid. One last thing: will you be coming by car?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Probably, yes. Is there parking at the museum?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Unfortunately we don't have our own car park. The nearest one is the multi-storey car park on Brook Street, which is about five minutes' walk away. There's also some street parking on Mill Lane, but it's limited to two hours, so it wouldn't really be long enough for the workshop.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: Brook Street, then. Thanks so much for your help.

listeningParts.title: A new exhibition on the origins of writing
listeningParts.contextDescription: A museum guide introduces visitors to a new exhibition about the earliest writing systems.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to Signs of the Past, our new exhibition on the beginnings of writing. My name's Ciara, and I'll be giving you a short introduction before you explore on your own. The exhibition has been three years in the making. The idea came about when we were offered a long-term loan of objects from a university collection that had been in storage for decades, and we realised we had the chance to tell a story that most museums can only tell in part.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: The exhibition is arranged in four rooms, and each one is devoted to a different region where writing developed early. You'll notice as soon as you go in that the lighting is quite dim. That isn't to create atmosphere, although it does. Many of the objects are made from organic materials, and strong light would fade and weaken them. So please give your eyes a minute to adjust. Photography is allowed throughout, but without flash, for the same reason.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Room One covers Mesopotamia, in what is now Iraq, where most specialists believe writing first appeared. The highlight here is a small clay tablet from the city of Uruk. It's an account of grain rations, and it's more than five thousand years old, which makes it the oldest object in the whole exhibition. In the same room, you'll find a table with replica cylinder seals. These were small carved stone cylinders that were rolled across wet clay to leave a design, a bit like a signature. You're welcome to pick the replicas up and roll them across the trays of modelling clay.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: In Room Two, we move to Egypt. People often think of hieroglyphs as the only Egyptian script, but in fact, for everyday purposes such as letters and accounts, scribes used a faster, joined-up script called hieratic, and we have some lovely examples on display. The material they usually wrote on, of course, was papyrus, which was made from a plant that grew along the Nile. There's a short film in this room that shows how papyrus sheets were made, using the same methods as in ancient times. It lasts about six minutes and runs continuously.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Room Three is devoted to China. The earliest Chinese writing that has survived is found on what are called oracle bones, from the Shang dynasty, around three thousand two hundred years ago. These were mostly the shoulder blades of oxen and the shells of turtles. A question would be addressed to the royal ancestors, for example whether a harvest would be good, and the bone was heated until it cracked. Specialists interpreted the cracks to predict the future, and the question, and sometimes the answer, was carved into the bone. Many of the characters can still be recognised by people who read Chinese today.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Finally, Room Four takes you across the Atlantic to the Maya of Central America. The centrepiece is a full-size replica of the Dresden Codex, one of only four Maya books known to have survived. It's made of bark paper and folds up like a screen. Next to it, there's an interactive display that converts your date of birth into the Maya calendar, and prints it out in Maya numbers for you to take home. Children love it, so there's sometimes a queue.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: A few practical points. The free audio guide is available through the museum's app, which you can download using the museum wi-fi, so you don't need to use your own data. The guide lasts about forty minutes. If you'd prefer a printed booklet, they cost three pounds at the shop. The exhibition is open every day until six, but on Thursdays it stays open until nine, and on those evenings there are short talks by curators at seven o'clock. Right, please do go on in and enjoy it.

listeningParts.title: A presentation on Linear B
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two history students, Zoe and Daniel, discuss their presentation on the decipherment of the Linear B script with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: So, Zoe, Daniel, your presentation's on Linear B. How's the planning going?

dialogue.speaker: Zoe
dialogue.text: Pretty well, I think. We've decided to tell it as a kind of detective story, because that's really what it was. We start in 1900, when Arthur Evans began excavating the palace at Knossos on Crete and found thousands of clay tablets covered in an unknown script.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: And we explain that Evans actually identified three scripts on Crete: a hieroglyphic one, Linear A and Linear B. Linear A still hasn't been deciphered, so we're only mentioning it briefly.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Sensible. One thing your audience might wonder about is how unbaked clay tablets survived for over three thousand years.

dialogue.speaker: Zoe
dialogue.text: Yes, we've got a slide on that. The tablets were only meant to be temporary records, so they weren't baked. Ironically, they survived because the palace was destroyed by fire, which baked them hard. Without that disaster, they'd have crumbled long ago.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. Now, how are you dividing the presentation between you?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: I'm doing the part about Alice Kober. I think she's often left out of the story, and she shouldn't be. She was an American classicist, and in the 1940s she showed that some words appeared in groups of three related forms, with different endings.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Her so-called triplets. And why did that matter?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: Because it proved the language had inflections, like Latin or Greek, where the ending of a word changes depending on its grammar. That meant you could start to work out which signs shared the same consonant or the same vowel, even without knowing the language. She did all this on thousands of handmade index cards, at a time when paper was in short supply. Sadly, she died in 1950, just two years before the breakthrough.

dialogue.speaker: Zoe
dialogue.text: And then I take over with Michael Ventris. What's amazing is that he wasn't a professional scholar at all. He was an architect, and he worked on the script in his spare time. He'd been fascinated by it since he heard Evans give a lecture when he was a schoolboy.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And what was his great insight?

dialogue.speaker: Zoe
dialogue.text: He built on Kober's method and made grids of the signs. For a long time, he was convinced the language was related to Etruscan, not Greek. But when he tried out some sound values on place names from Crete, like Knossos, the words suddenly looked like an early form of Greek. He announced it on BBC radio in 1952, and many people were sceptical at first.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: What convinced them was a tablet found at Pylos, on the Greek mainland. It had pictures of pots with three legs, and the word next to them, using Ventris's values, read as the Greek word for tripod. That was hard to argue with.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Excellent. Do you deal with what the tablets actually say? People often hope for poetry or history.

dialogue.speaker: Zoe
dialogue.text: Yes, and that's the slight disappointment. They're almost all administrative records: inventories of sheep, wool, chariot wheels, and offerings to the gods. But we want to argue that that's actually valuable, because it tells us how the palace economy worked in detail.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: I'd agree. You might add that the decipherment pushed back the history of the Greek language by several centuries. Now, a word on timing. Your draft runs to twenty-five minutes, and you've only got fifteen.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: We know. We were thinking of cutting the section on Linear A completely.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: I'd keep one slide on it, actually. It's a nice way to end, showing that there are still mysteries to solve. Cut some of the background on Evans instead. And practise with a timer.

dialogue.speaker: Zoe
dialogue.text: Okay. And should we mention that Ventris died very young?

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Briefly, yes. He was killed in a car accident in 1956, aged only thirty-four, the same year that his book with John Chadwick was published. It's a moving detail, but don't let it take over. Send me the revised slides by Friday.

listeningParts.title: Reading the Maya glyphs
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in an archaeology course on how the Maya writing system was deciphered.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning. Today we're looking at one of the great intellectual achievements of the twentieth century: the decipherment of Maya writing. The Maya of southern Mexico and Central America developed the most complete writing system in the ancient Americas, one that could record anything their language could express. It was in use from at least the third century BC until after the Spanish conquest in the sixteenth century.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Most surviving Maya writing is carved in stone, on monuments, temple stairways and altars, but the Maya also painted texts on pottery and wrote books. These books, which we call codices, were made from bark, which was pounded into sheets, coated with a fine layer of lime plaster, and folded like a screen. Thousands must once have existed. Only four survive today, and the best known is the Dresden Codex, named after the German city where it's kept. It contains remarkably accurate astronomical tables, including calculations of the movements of the planet Venus and predictions of eclipses.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Why did so few books survive? Partly because bark paper decays quickly in a tropical climate. But there was also deliberate destruction. In 1562, a Spanish friar named Diego de Landa, who later became Bishop of Yucatán, ordered the burning of a large number of Maya books at the town of Maní, because he regarded them as works of the devil. The great irony is that Landa also wrote an account of Maya life, which contains what he believed to be the Maya alphabet. This document would eventually become a key to the decipherment, although it lay forgotten in a Spanish library until the nineteenth century.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The problem with Landa's alphabet was that it didn't seem to work. For decades, scholars tried to read texts with it and failed. The reason, we now know, is that the Maya script is not an alphabet. It is what we call a logosyllabic system. Some signs, called logograms, represent whole words, while others represent syllables, usually a consonant followed by a vowel. When Landa asked his informant to write the Spanish letters, the scribe wrote the Maya syllable that sounded most like the name of each letter.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The breakthrough came from an unexpected direction. In 1952, a young Soviet scholar, Yuri Knorozov, published an article arguing that Landa's signs should be read as syllables. Knorozov never visited a Maya site until very late in his life; he worked from published drawings in Leningrad. His ideas were rejected for many years, especially by the British scholar Eric Thompson, who was the leading authority in the field and believed the glyphs were mainly symbolic rather than phonetic.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The second great step was taken by Tatiana Proskouriakoff, a Russian-born American who had trained as an architect. In 1960, she studied the dates on monuments at the site of Piedras Negras and noticed that they fell into groups, each covering a period no longer than a human lifetime. She concluded that the inscriptions recorded the births, accessions and deaths of real rulers. Until then, most scholars had believed the texts dealt only with the calendar, astronomy and religion. Suddenly, the Maya had a political history, with named kings and queens, wars and alliances.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: From the 1970s onwards, progress was rapid. At a famous conference held at Palenque in 1973, a small group of researchers worked out the sequence of the city's rulers in a single afternoon, including its most famous king, Pakal. Today, specialists can read the great majority of known Maya inscriptions, although some signs are still uncertain.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Before we finish, I want to mention numbers. The Maya counted in base twenty rather than base ten, and they wrote numbers using just three symbols: a dot for one, a bar for five, and a shell to represent zero. That makes them one of the very few ancient peoples to have developed the concept of zero independently. And finally, it's worth remembering that the Maya did not disappear. Millions of people speak Maya languages today, and some are now learning to read and write the script of their ancestors. Next week, we'll look at the Maya calendar in more detail.

readingPassages.title: Clay, reeds and the first scribes
paragraphs: Writing is so central to modern life that it is easy to forget how recent an invention it is. Human beings have been speaking for tens of thousands of years, perhaps far longer, but the earliest true writing appeared only about five thousand years ago. Most scholars agree that it emerged first in southern Mesopotamia, the flat, fertile land between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers in what is now Iraq. Writing was also invented independently in at least two other places, China and Mesoamerica, and possibly in Egypt, but the Mesopotamian system, later known as cuneiform, has the longest documented history of development.

The setting for this development was the city of Uruk, which by the late fourth millennium BC was one of the largest settlements in the world, with a population that may have reached several tens of thousands. Its great temples controlled vast quantities of grain, livestock, textiles and labour, and the officials who managed these resources faced a problem that memory alone could not solve: how to keep track of who had delivered what, who was owed rations, and how many animals were in each flock. The oldest tablets from Uruk, dating from around 3200 BC, are overwhelmingly concerned with exactly these matters. Rather than poetry, prayers or history, they record quantities of barley, beer and sheep.

Where did the idea of writing come from? One influential theory was developed by the archaeologist Denise Schmandt-Besserat, who studied thousands of small clay objects, known as tokens, found at sites across the Near East. These tokens, in shapes such as cones, spheres and discs, had been used for several thousand years before writing appeared, and she argued that each shape stood for a particular quantity of a particular commodity. To guarantee a transaction, tokens were sometimes sealed inside hollow clay balls, called envelopes, and their shapes were pressed into the outer surface so that the contents could be checked without breaking the ball. Eventually, Schmandt-Besserat suggested, people realised that the marks on the outside made the tokens themselves unnecessary. Not all scholars accept every part of her account, but most agree that writing grew out of earlier systems of counting and recording.

The earliest signs were mostly pictures, drawn into wet clay with a pointed tool: an ear of grain for barley, a jar for beer, the head of an ox for cattle. Signs for numbers were impressed separately. Over the following centuries, however, scribes began to make their marks by pressing the end of a cut reed into the clay rather than drawing with it. This was quicker, but it produced wedge-shaped strokes, and gradually the pictures became abstract groups of wedges that bore little resemblance to the objects they had once represented. It is from these marks that the script takes its modern name: cuneiform comes from cuneus, the Latin word for a wedge.

An even more important change was the use of signs for their sound rather than their meaning. Sumerian, the language of the early scribes, had many short words, and a sign for one word could be borrowed to write another word, or part of a word, that sounded the same. This principle, often compared to a rebus puzzle, allowed scribes to record personal names, grammatical endings and, eventually, any sentence of the spoken language. By around the middle of the third millennium BC, cuneiform was being used for letters, laws, hymns and literary texts as well as accounts. Among the most famous works later written in cuneiform is the Epic of Gilgamesh, the story of a king of Uruk who searches for immortality.

Learning to write was difficult and took years. Trainee scribes, who were mostly boys, studied at schools known in Sumerian as the edubba, or 'tablet house'. They copied long lists of signs and words again and again, often on small round tablets that could be smoothed and reused. Thousands of these practice tablets have survived, some with the teacher's model on one side and a pupil's imperfect copy on the other. Because clay is easily damaged when wet but extremely durable once dry, and even more so when baked, enormous numbers of cuneiform documents have come down to us, sometimes preserved by the very fires that destroyed the buildings in which they were stored.

Cuneiform proved remarkably adaptable. Over roughly three thousand years, it was used to write a number of quite different languages, including Akkadian, the language of the Babylonians and Assyrians, as well as Hittite in what is now Turkey and Elamite in what is now Iran. For long periods, Akkadian written in cuneiform served as an international language of diplomacy; in the fourteenth century BC, even the rulers of Egypt corresponded with other kings in this script, as shown by the clay letters discovered at Amarna. Gradually, though, cuneiform was replaced by alphabetic scripts written with ink on softer materials, and the last known tablets, which record astronomical observations, date from the first century AD.

The script was then entirely forgotten for nearly two thousand years. Its decipherment in the nineteenth century relied heavily on long inscriptions in more than one language, such as the one carved for the Persian king Darius I on a cliff at Behistun, which the British officer Henry Rawlinson copied at considerable personal risk. In 1857, to test whether the decipherment was reliable, the Royal Asiatic Society in London sent copies of a newly discovered inscription to four scholars, including Rawlinson, and asked them to translate it independently. When their sealed translations were opened and compared, they agreed closely enough to convince most sceptics that the long-dead language could genuinely be read again.

readingPassages.title: The silent script of the Indus
paragraphs: In the 1920s, excavations at Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, in what is now Pakistan, revealed a civilisation that had been completely forgotten. At its height, between about 2600 and 1900 BC, the Indus or Harappan civilisation covered an area larger than ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia combined. Its cities were laid out on carefully planned grids, with covered drains, large public buildings and houses built from bricks of standardised proportions. Its traders used a uniform system of weights across hundreds of kilometres. Yet, unlike the Egyptians and Mesopotamians, the people of the Indus left no texts that anyone can read, and the language they spoke remains unknown.

This is not because they did not write. Archaeologists have found around four thousand objects bearing signs of the Indus script. The great majority are small square seals carved from soft stone, usually showing an animal, most often a one-horned creature that excavators named the 'unicorn', beneath a short line of signs. Other inscriptions appear on pottery, copper tablets and small clay tags that were probably attached to bundles of goods. What is striking is how brief all of these texts are. The average inscription contains only about five signs, and even the longest have fewer than thirty.

The brevity of the inscriptions is only the first of several difficulties facing anyone who hopes to read them. A second is the absence of a bilingual text, an inscription that gives the same message in a known language as well as in the Indus script. Such texts were crucial in the decipherment of Egyptian hieroglyphs and cuneiform. A third problem is that we do not know which language family the Indus language belonged to, or whether any modern language is descended from it. Successful decipherments have usually depended on at least one of these clues; for the Indus script, none is clearly available.

Nevertheless, careful analysis has established some facts. In 1977, the Indian scholar Iravatham Mahadevan published a concordance, a complete catalogue of the known inscriptions and the signs in them, which identified around four hundred distinct signs. This number is important. Alphabets typically have between twenty and forty letters, and purely syllabic scripts rarely more than about a hundred signs, whereas systems in which signs stand for whole words, such as Chinese, need thousands. A total of around four hundred suggests that, like cuneiform, the Indus script combined signs for words with signs for sounds. Studies of the spacing of signs, which are often squeezed together at the left-hand end of an inscription, also show that the script was normally written from right to left.

Beyond such conclusions, there is little agreement. Dozens of decipherments have been announced, most of which identify the language with one of the major language families of modern South Asia. The Finnish scholar Asko Parpola, among others, has argued for many years that the language was an early form of Dravidian, the family that today includes Tamil and is spoken mainly in southern India. Others have proposed early forms of Sanskrit or entirely different languages. Because the history of the Indian subcontinent is a sensitive political subject, these debates have sometimes become heated, and claims are not always judged on purely scholarly grounds.

In 2004, the debate took a dramatic turn when three researchers, Steve Farmer, Richard Sproat and Michael Witzel, published a paper arguing that the Indus signs were not writing at all. They pointed out that the inscriptions were extraordinarily short, that many signs appeared only once, and that no example had been found of the kind of long text that literate societies usually produce. In their view, the signs were a system of symbols, perhaps related to religion, family groups or political identity, which could convey meaning without representing a spoken language.

This provocative claim prompted a response from a team led by the computer scientist Rajesh Rao, who in 2009 published a statistical study in the journal Science. The team measured how predictable each sign was given the sign that came before it, and compared the result with known languages and with non-linguistic systems such as DNA sequences and computer code. The Indus script, they reported, fell within the range of linguistic systems, suggesting that it did encode language. Their critics replied that the measure could not reliably distinguish writing from other kinds of structured symbol systems, and the question remains open.

What might settle the matter? Most specialists believe that progress depends on new discoveries. In the 1990s, excavators at Dholavira in western India found a row of ten large signs that had apparently once been fixed above a gateway, perhaps as a kind of public notice, which shows that longer and more public inscriptions may yet be found. Indus seals have also been discovered in Mesopotamia, and Mesopotamian texts refer to a distant land called Meluhha, which many scholars identify with the Indus region. If a bilingual document from this long-distance trade were ever unearthed, it could do for the Indus script what the great trilingual inscriptions did for the scripts of Egypt and Mesopotamia.

readingPassages.title: Did writing change the way we think?
paragraphs: Few inventions have been credited with as much influence as writing. It has been said to have made possible history, science, law, philosophy and the modern state. A bolder claim, however, is that writing did not merely give people a new tool but changed the way human beings think. This idea has been argued, attacked and refined for more than half a century, and it remains one of the most interesting questions in the study of the human past.

The debate has a surprisingly ancient starting point. In Plato's dialogue Phaedrus, written in the fourth century BC, Socrates tells a story in which the Egyptian god Theuth presents his invention of writing to King Thamus, claiming that it will improve memory and wisdom. The king disagrees. Writing, he says, will make people forgetful, because they will rely on marks outside themselves instead of their own memories, and it will give them the appearance of wisdom without the reality. It is an irony often noted that we know of this criticism of writing only because Plato wrote it down.

The modern version of the debate began with scholars of oral poetry. In the 1920s and 1930s, the American classicist Milman Parry argued that the Homeric epics, the Iliad and the Odyssey, showed clear signs of having been composed without writing. Their repeated phrases, such as 'swift-footed Achilles', were not decoration but tools that allowed a singer to compose verse rapidly during performance. To test this theory, Parry and his assistant Albert Lord recorded living oral poets in Yugoslavia, some of whom could perform poems of many thousands of lines. Their work suggested that oral cultures possessed sophisticated techniques of memory and composition that literate cultures had largely lost.

Building on such research, several scholars in the 1960s and later proposed that literacy had transformed human thought. The anthropologist Jack Goody argued that writing made possible new intellectual tools, particularly lists and tables, which allowed information to be detached from its context, compared and reorganised. Walter Ong, in his influential book Orality and Literacy, published in 1982, went further, claiming that writing 'restructures consciousness'. In Ong's account, oral thinking tends to be practical, concrete and closely tied to human situations, whereas literate thinking is more abstract, analytical and detached.

These claims were soon challenged. In a study published in 1981, the psychologists Sylvia Scribner and Michael Cole investigated the Vai people of Liberia, some of whom had learned to read and write an indigenous script outside any school. This allowed the researchers to separate the effects of literacy from those of formal education, which earlier studies had confused. They found that literacy alone did not produce general improvements in abstract reasoning. Instead, it was associated with specific skills linked to the particular ways the script was used, such as writing letters. Schooling, not writing as such, seemed to explain many of the differences that had been attributed to literacy.

More recently, neuroscience has added a different kind of evidence. The French researcher Stanislas Dehaene has shown that reading relies on a small region of the brain's visual system, which in literate people becomes specialised for recognising letters and words. Because writing is far too recent for the brain to have evolved specifically for it, Dehaene proposes that reading 'recycles' circuits that originally evolved for other purposes, such as recognising objects and faces. Learning to read, in other words, physically changes the brain, although this tells us more about perception than about the higher forms of thought that Goody and Ong had in mind.

In my view, the strongest versions of the argument that writing transformed the mind should be rejected. They tended to portray people in oral cultures as less capable of abstract or logical thought, a conclusion that is not supported by the evidence and that sat uncomfortably close to older prejudices about so-called primitive societies. The oral poets recorded by Parry and Lord, after all, were performing feats of memory and composition that few literate people could equal. Yet it would be equally mistaken to conclude that writing changed nothing. Writing allows ideas to be stored, compared and criticised across generations, and over time this has transformed what societies can know, even if it has not transformed the individual mind.

The debate has acquired fresh relevance in the digital age. Many people now worry that search engines and smartphones are weakening memory and attention, in much the same way that Thamus feared writing would. It is tempting to dismiss such fears, as Thamus has been dismissed, as the familiar anxiety that accompanies every new technology. In my view, that would be too easy. The history of writing suggests that new technologies of information rarely make us more or less intelligent, but they do change which skills a society values and which it allows to decline. The real question is not whether our tools change us, but whether we choose those changes wisely.
